paragraphs.heading: The Greco-Roman world
paragraphs.text: Classical antiquity is the stretch of European cultural history from the 8th century BC to the 5th century AD. It came after the Greek Dark Ages and gave way to late antiquity. At its centre were ancient Greece and Rome, two intertwined civilizations known together as the Greco-Roman world. In this era they flourished, held great influence over much of Europe, North Africa and West Asia, and helped shape the culture of the Mediterranean.

paragraphs.heading: Where it starts and ends
paragraphs.text: By convention the era opens with Homer's epic poetry, the earliest recorded of its kind in Greek, and closes in 476 AD, when the Western Roman Empire fell. Homer is usually placed in the 8th or 7th century BC, and the first Greek alphabetic inscriptions appear in the first half of the 8th century. The traditional founding date of the ancient Olympic Games, 776 BC, falls in the same period. A span this long and wide covers many different cultures and periods.

paragraphs.heading: The Archaic period
paragraphs.text: The Archaic period followed the Greek Dark Ages and brought big advances in political theory. It also saw the beginnings of democracy, philosophy, theatre and poetry, and the revival of writing, which had been lost in the Dark Ages. Pottery tracks the change: the geometric style gave way to an Orientalizing style that drew on Egypt, Phoenicia and Syria. Later came black-figure pottery, which began in Corinth in the 7th century BC, and then red-figure, developed by the Andokides Painter around 530 BC.

paragraphs.heading: From kings to a republic
paragraphs.text: Legend says Rome was founded on 21 April 753 BC by the twins Romulus and Remus. Archaeology does find the earliest traces of people living at the Roman Forum from the mid-8th century BC, though the Palatine Hill may have been settled as early as the 10th century BC. According to legend, the seventh and last king was Tarquinius Superbus, who was expelled from Rome in 510 BC. In 509 BC the Senate voted never again to allow a king and turned Rome into a republic.

paragraphs.heading: Classical Greece
paragraphs.text: The classical period of Greece covers most of the 5th and 4th centuries BC, running from 510 BC, when tyranny ended in Athens, until Alexander the Great died in 323 BC. The Greco-Persian Wars (499–449 BC) freed Greece, Macedon, Thrace and Ionia from Persian rule and left Athens dominant in the Delian League. That brought conflict with Sparta and the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC), which Sparta won. Then, in 371 BC, two Theban generals, Epaminondas and Pelopidas, won the Battle of Leuctra, ending Spartan supremacy, and Thebes led Greece until the rising power of Macedon ended its dominance in 346 BC.

paragraphs.heading: Macedon and Alexander
paragraphs.text: Under Philip II (359–336 BC), Macedon expanded into the lands of the Paeonians, Thracians and Illyrians. His son, Alexander the Great, briefly carried Macedonian power over the central Greek city-states and across the Persian Empire, including Egypt and lands reaching the fringes of India. By convention, classical Greece ends with Alexander's death in 323 BC, when his empire broke up and was divided among the Diadochi. Greece entered the Hellenistic period with the growing power of Macedon and Alexander's conquests.

paragraphs.heading: A lasting foundation
paragraphs.text: Greek culture, plus some influence from the ancient Near East, formed the base for art, philosophy, society and education around the Mediterranean and Near East up to the time of the Roman emperors. The Romans kept, imitated and spread this culture across Europe. That Greco-Roman base has shaped language, politics, law, education, science, literature, art and architecture in the West and, through the West, the modern world. Surviving pieces of classical culture helped spark a revival starting in the 14th century, later called the Renaissance, and neo-classical revivals followed in the 18th and 19th centuries.
